newsitem.title: UK: EU faces tricky balance on grain exports - trader.
newsitem.headline: EU faces tricky balance on grain exports - trader.

text.p: The European Union (EU) may lose traditional outlets for grain exports as it tries to strike a fine balance between surpluses and stubbornly high internal prices, a leading French trader said.

Etienne Caen of Louis Dreyfus said that the EU, with practically no intervention stocks to play with, lacked the necessary weapon to use to depress prices that are still hovering at five to 15 percent above intervention levels.
"A delicate balance has to be reached, but in the meantime, business opportunities might be lost," Caen said in a monthly newsletter of the Grain and Feed Trade Association (GAFTA).
French traders were enraged last weekend when Egypt, a regular buyer of French wheat, covered most of a 600,000-tonne tender from Australia and Argentina.
Caen said a bumper crop this year should allow the EU to export at least as much as the 28.8 million tonnes of grains shipped in 1994/95.
But even this was modest given that it had the right under WTO rules to export up to 29.7 million tonnes of subsidised grain in 1996/97.
"One fears that end-season stocks in the European Union will unnecessarily build up," he said.
One impediment was that the EU Commission, fearful of a rift with the United States over high subsidies, continued to track U.S. prices when setting restitution levels.
But Argentina had a bigger presence in international wheat markets at prices $15-20 below soft red winter wheat.

EU wheat prices meanwhile would "probably not go down to intervention level" as farmers, their pockets filled with compensation and area aid payments, were likely to carry stocks into the next season.
"Much will depend on the outlook for the next crop during April/May," Caen said.
A decline in 1996/97 was likely in imports by Mediterranean and Middle East countries and possibly by Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, all traditional destinations for EU grain.
But imports by Southeast Asia would remain high, he said.
